module_title: SAT Jurisdiction, Collective Investment Schemes & Sahara Judgment
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams and UPSC Law Optional, this level covers the appellate hierarchy of the securities market, SEBI's sweeping powers over unlisted companies, and the monumental 'Sahara' case that redefined Collective Investment Schemes.

core_concepts.title: Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT)
core_concepts.description:
SAT is a specialized statutory body established under Section 15K of the SEBI Act to hear appeals against orders passed by SEBI, the PFRDA (Pension Fund regulator), and the IRDAI (Insurance regulator).
- Jurisdiction: SAT acts as the first appellate authority against SEBI's penalties or directions.
- Supreme Court Appeal (Section 15Z): Any person aggrieved by a decision of SAT can appeal directly to the **Supreme Court of India** within 60 days. 
- Limitation: The appeal to the SC can ONLY be filed on a **'Question of Law'**, not on questions of fact.

core_concepts.title: Collective Investment Schemes (CIS) - Section 11AA
core_concepts.description:
A scheme where contributions made by investors are pooled and utilized for the purpose of the scheme, with the investors expecting to receive profits/income, and the property is managed on behalf of the investors (who do not have day-to-day control).
- Mutual funds are exempt from CIS rules as they have their own regulations. 
- Deemed CIS: Any scheme offering a return on investment corpus of **₹100 Crore or more**, which is not registered under any specific law, is legally 'deemed' to be a CIS and falls strictly under SEBI's jurisdiction.

core_concepts.title: The Sahara Judgment (Sahara India Real Estate Corp. v. SEBI, 2012)
core_concepts.description:
The most defining case of SEBI's jurisdictional reach over unlisted companies.
- The Scam: Two unlisted Sahara companies raised ₹24,000 Crores by issuing Optionally Fully Convertible Debentures (OFCDs) to over 30 million people, claiming it was a 'private placement' outside SEBI's jurisdiction.
- The Law: Section 67 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now Sec 42 of the 2013 Act) stated that offering securities to **50 or more persons** (now 200) automatically makes it a 'Public Issue', regardless of whether the company is listed or unlisted.
- Supreme Court Ruling: The SC held that since Sahara issued OFCDs to millions, it was a public issue. SEBI has absolute jurisdiction to protect investors in public issues. Sahara was ordered to refund the entire amount with 15% interest.

core_concepts.title: Recent Reforms: SCORES 2.0 & T+0 Settlement
core_concepts.description:
- SCORES 2.0: SEBI's revamped online Complaint Redressal System, mandating a strict 21-day auto-routed timeline for resolving investor grievances.
- T+0 Settlement (2024/2025 rollout): Moving away from the traditional T+2 or T+1 settlement cycles, SEBI introduced a T+0 (same-day) settlement framework for equity cash markets, drastically reducing counterparty risk and increasing market liquidity.

important_entities.name: Disgorgement of Profits
important_entities.key_fact: A severe equitable remedy used by SEBI.
important_entities.significance: Under Section 11B of the SEBI Act, SEBI has the power to order 'Disgorgement'. This means forcing an insider trader or a fraudulent entity to surrender all the illicit profits they made from the illegal transaction. It is not a penalty; it is the confiscation of ill-gotten gains to restore the status quo.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: If a question asks: 'Which court handles appeals against the orders of the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT)?' Do NOT select the High Court. Section 15Z of the SEBI Act provides a direct statutory appeal from SAT to the **Supreme Court of India** on questions of law. Civil courts are strictly barred from entertaining suits relating to SEBI matters.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Any unregistered scheme pooling ₹100 Crores or more is automatically deemed a Collective Investment Scheme, bringing the CBI/Police/SEBI machinery into action.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Mains, when discussing regulatory overreach versus investor protection, cite the **Sahara Judgment (2012)** to demonstrate how the Supreme Court validated SEBI's authority over unlisted companies to protect retail investors in mass 'private placements'.
